title: Lamentations 4:1–10
context: Lamentations 4 is the fourth of the book’s acrostic laments. Its twenty-two verses begin with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. In 4:1–10 the poet, speaking as an eyewitness of Jerusalem’s fall, mourns the change that has come over the city. Its gold has grown dim, the stones of the sanctuary are scattered in the streets, and the precious sons of Zion are treated like clay pots. Children cry for bread and water, those raised in luxury lie on ash heaps, and nobles once radiant are now blackened and wasted by hunger. The poet says that Jerusalem’s iniquity is greater than Sodom’s, which was overthrown in a moment, and that those killed by the sword were better off than those who wasted away from famine. The unit ends with the most terrible picture of the siege, of mothers driven to eat their own children (4:10). That verse is a sober witness to the horror, set beside the covenant warning in Deuteronomy 28:53–57 and the earlier lament in 2:20. Both traditions read this unit with grief, not curiosity, as a lament over judgment that came after long warning.

verses.text: How the gold has become dim! The most pure gold has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are poured out at the head of every street.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet laments that the gold has grown dim and the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in every street. Arminian readers see the tragic loss of what was precious and holy, which the people’s unfaithfulness brought about.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the dimmed gold as a picture of Zion’s lost glory. Both traditions read the stones of the sanctuary as either the temple’s actual stones or, as some suggest, a figure for the people themselves, and they hold the image open.

verses.text: The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how they are esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says Zion’s precious sons, once worth fine gold, are now regarded as clay pots made by a potter. Arminians see the painful reversal of the people’s worth in the eyes of the world, as judgment strips away their honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the contrast between gold and clay as showing how far Zion has fallen. Both traditions note the potter image elsewhere in Jeremiah (chapters 18–19), and they read this verse as a lament rather than a doctrine.

verses.text: Even the jackals offer their breast. They nurse their young ones. But the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says even jackals nurse their young, but the daughter of my people has become cruel like ostriches. Arminian readers see the famine breaking down the natural bonds of care, which shows how terrible the siege had become.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing the effects of judgment on human relationships. Both traditions note that the ostrich was proverbial for neglecting its young (compare Job 39:13–16), and they read the verse with compassion for those who suffered.

verses.text: The tongue of the nursing child clings to the roof of his mouth for thirst. The young children ask for bread, and no one breaks it for them.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says nursing children’s tongues cling to their mouths from thirst, and young children ask for bread that no one breaks for them. Arminians see the innocent suffering in the siege, which moves the poet to grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the suffering of children as one of the deepest sorrows of judgment. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as a call to compassion and to recognizing the cost of the nation’s sin.

verses.text: Those who ate delicacies are desolate in the streets. Those who were brought up in purple embrace dunghills.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says those who ate delicacies are desolate in the streets, and those raised in purple cling to ash heaps. Arminian readers see the reversal of fortune that came on the wealthy, who lost everything in the city’s fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as showing that judgment fell on rich and poor alike. Both traditions note that purple was a sign of wealth and status, and they read the verse as part of the poet’s lament over Zion’s ruin.

verses.text: For the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown as in a moment. No hands were laid on her.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than Sodom’s sin, which was overthrown in a moment without human hands. Arminians see the poet acknowledging the depth of Jerusalem’s guilt, made worse by her privileges as God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the comparison as stressing the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness. Both traditions note that Sodom’s quick destruction (Genesis 19) is contrasted with Jerusalem’s long suffering, and they read the verse as confession, not exaggeration.

verses.text: Her nobles were purer than snow. They were whiter than milk. They were more ruddy in body than rubies. Their polishing was like sapphire.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says Zion’s nobles were purer than snow, whiter than milk, and more ruddy than rubies. Arminian readers see a description of their former health and beauty, which makes their present condition more painful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as setting up the contrast in verse 8. Both traditions note that the word rendered nobles may refer to princes or to consecrated persons, and they hold the identification lightly.

verses.text: Their appearance is blacker than a coal. They are not known in the streets. Their skin clings to their bones. It is withered. It has become like wood.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says their appearance is now blacker than coal, they are unrecognized in the streets, and their skin clings to their bones. Arminians see the devastating effects of famine, which left even the noble unrecognizable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a sober picture of suffering under judgment. Both traditions read it with compassion, as the poet’s honest witness to what the siege did to the people.

verses.text: Those who are killed with the sword are better than those who are killed with hunger; for these pine away, stricken through, for lack of the fruits of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says those killed by the sword were better off than those who died of hunger, wasting away for lack of food. Arminian readers see the terrible slowness of death by famine, which the poet judges worse than a quick death in battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as expressing the depth of the city’s agony. Both traditions read it as lament, naming the horror of the siege without turning it into a theological argument.

verses.text: The hands of the pitiful women have boiled their own children. They were their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says compassionate women boiled their own children, who became their food when the city was destroyed. Arminians receive this verse with grief and silence, seeing it as the deepest horror of the siege, which the covenant warnings had foretold (Deuteronomy 28:53–57).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse soberly, as a witness to how far suffering can drive people under judgment. Both traditions note the earlier lament in 2:20 and avoid elaboration, treating the verse as a call to mourning and repentance.
